claim: Mature neocortical pyramidal cells functionally express two sodium channel (NaV) isoforms: NaV1.2 and NaV1.6.
source: Mature neocortical pyramidal cells functionally express two sodium channel (NaV) isoforms: NaV1.2 and NaV1.6.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the expression pattern of sodium channels in mature neocortical pyramidal cells.

claim: NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 are differentially localized to pyramidal cell compartments.
source: These isoforms are differentially localized to pyramidal cell compartments, and as such are thought to contribute to different aspects of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior literature and is a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Aryl sulfonamide-based molecule (ASC) inhibitors exhibit state-dependent block of both NaV1.2 and NaV1.6.
source: Here, we leveraged aryl sulfonamide-based molecule (ASC) inhibitors of NaV channels that exhibit state-dependent block of both NaV1.2 and NaV1.6, along with knock-in mice with changes in NaV1.2 or NaV1.6 structure that prevents ASC binding.
evidence: This describes the pharmacological tool used in the study and its mechanism of action.

claim: Knock-in mice with changes in NaV1.2 or NaV1.6 structure prevent ASC binding.
source: Here, we leveraged aryl sulfonamide-based molecule (ASC) inhibitors of NaV channels that exhibit state-dependent block of both NaV1.2 and NaV1.6, along with knock-in mice with changes in NaV1.2 or NaV1.6 structure that prevents ASC binding.
evidence: This describes the genetic tool developed for the study.

claim: Block of NaV1.6 decreases neuronal action potential output.
source: Remarkably, block of each isoform had contrasting—and in some situations, opposing—effects on neuronal action potential output, with NaV1.6 block decreasing and NaV1.2 block increasing output.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Block of NaV1.2 increases neuronal action potential output.
source: Remarkably, block of each isoform had contrasting—and in some situations, opposing—effects on neuronal action potential output, with NaV1.6 block decreasing and NaV1.2 block increasing output.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: NaV channels are critical for all aspects of neuronal excitability, from action potential initiation to axonal propagation, transmitter release, and dendritic excitability.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV) are critical for all aspects of neuronal excitability, from action potential (AP) initiation to axonal propagation, transmitter release, and dendritic excitability (Meeks and Mennerick, 2007; Shu et al., 2007; Palmer and Stuart, 2006; Spratt et al., 2021; Spratt et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In mature neocortical pyramidal cells, electrogenesis and subsequent propagation of APs is systematically regulated with NaV recruitment first initiated in the axon initial segment (AIS).
source: In mature neocortical pyramidal cells, electrogenesis and subsequent propagation of APs is systematically regulated with NaV recruitment first initiated in the axon initial segment (AIS), with forward propagation along the axon and backpropagation into soma and dendrites (Shu et al., 2007; Palmer and Stuart, 2006; Baranauskas et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NaV1.6 predominates in the AIS, with the highest membrane density in the AP initiation region of the AIS most distal to the soma.
source: In the AIS, NaV1.6 predominates, with the highest membrane density in the AP initiation region of the AIS most distal to the soma.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature describing channel localization.

claim: NaV1.2 has higher relative membrane density in the proximal AIS.
source: NaV1.2, by contrast, has higher relative membrane density in the proximal AIS (Shu et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2014; Ye et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2008; Jenkins and Bender, 2025).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature describing channel localization.

claim: NaV1.6 appears enriched at nodes of Ranvier and terminals along the axon.
source: Along the axon, NaV1.6 appears enriched at nodes of Ranvier and terminals (Caldwell et al., 2000; Kaplan et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The somatic and perisomatic membrane expresses equal levels of NaV1.6 and NaV1.2.
source: Thus, excised patches from this region can provide insight into the block of both isoforms. Acute coronal slices containing mPFC were prepared from WT or Scn8a/2aSR/SR mice, and nucleated patches were excised from layer 5 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on current models from prior literature.

claim: Dendritic regions more distal to the soma are enriched exclusively with NaV1.2.
source: Somatodendritic densities are far lower, and current models suggest that the somatic and perisomatic membrane expresses equal levels of NaV1.6 and NaV1.2, whereas dendritic regions more distal to the soma are enriched exclusively with NaV1.2 (Spratt et al., 2021; Spratt et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2024; Fleidervish et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Conditional knockout of Scn2a results in an increase in NaV1.6 expression.
source: Similar to NaV1.2 conditional knockout, where NaV1.6 is upregulated, knockout of NaV1.6 results in an increase in NaV1.2 expression, at least in the AIS.
evidence: This statement describes compensatory changes observed in genetic knockout models.

claim: Aryl sulfonamide compounds (ASCs) potently bind activated NaV isoforms, resulting in a stabilization of the inactivated state.
source: Aryl sulfonamide compounds (ASCs) constitute a unique class of NaV inhibitors that potently bind activated NaV isoforms, resulting in a stabilization of the inactivated state (Ahuja et al., 2015; Goodchild et al., 2024; Johnson et al., 2024; Johnson et al., 2022; Roecker et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing ASC mechanism of action.

claim: The ASC binding pocket is shielded from ASCs when channels are closed due to the positioning of the S4 voltage sensing domain.
source: The binding pocket is shielded from ASCs when channels are closed due to the positioning of the S4 voltage sensing domain, but is bound rapidly by ASMs when exposed.
evidence: This describes the structural basis for state-dependent binding of ASCs.

claim: ASC unbinding is promoted by strong hyperpolarization, but occurs much more slowly at physiological voltages.
source: Unbinding is promoted by strong hyperpolarization, but occurs much more slowly at physiological voltages (e.g., tau of 102–103 s at –80 and –40 mV, respectively) (Ahuja et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation describing ASC unbinding kinetics.

claim: In spiking neurons, ASC block exhibits use dependence.
source: In spiking neurons, this essentially imparts use dependence to ASC block (Ahuja et al., 2015), as the probability of channel block will increase in proportion with AP rates.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and describes the functional consequence of ASC binding kinetics.

claim: ASCs exhibit high potency for NaV1.2, NaV1.6, and NaV1.7.
source: ASCs exhibit high potency for a subset of NaV isoforms: NaV1.2, NaV1.6, and NaV1.7 (Ahuja et al., 2015; Goodchild et al., 2024; Johnson et al., 2024; Johnson et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing ASC selectivity.

claim: NaV1.2, NaV1.6, and NaV1.7 share sequence homology at the binding pocket, each containing a tyrosine–tryptophan (YW) motif that helps stabilize ASC binding.
source: These isoforms share sequence homology at the binding pocket, each containing a tyrosine–tryptophan (YW) motif that helps stabilize ASC binding.
evidence: This describes the structural basis for ASC selectivity.

claim: NaV1.1 and NaV1.3 harbor a serine–arginine (SR) sequence at the same site as the YW motif in other isoforms.
source: By contrast, NaV1.1 and NaV1.3 harbor a serine–arginine (SR) sequence at the same site.
evidence: This describes the sequence difference that explains differential ASC binding.

claim: Mutagenesis of NaV1.7 from YW to SR results in a 145-fold decrease in ASC binding without affecting channel biophysical properties.
source: Mutagenesis of NaV1.7 from YW to SR results in a 145-fold decrease in ASC binding without affecting channel biophysical properties (Ahuja et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation describing prior mutagenesis experiments.

claim: GNE-4076 IC50 for wildtype NaV1.2 is 5.1 nM.
source: Dose–response curves revealed an IC50 of 5.1 nM for wildtype NaV1.2 that increases 365-fold to 1861 nM for mutant SR channels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GNE-4076 IC50 for SR mutant NaV1.2 is 1861 nM, representing a 365-fold increase compared to wildtype.
source: Dose–response curves revealed an IC50 of 5.1 nM for wildtype NaV1.2 that increases 365-fold to 1861 nM for mutant SR channels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GNE-4076 IC50 for wildtype NaV1.6 is 184 nM.
source: For NaV1.6 channels, GNE-4076 IC50 increased 475-fold from 184 nM to 87 μM with the SR mutant (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GNE-4076 IC50 for SR mutant NaV1.6 is 87 μM, representing a 475-fold increase compared to wildtype.
source: For NaV1.6 channels, GNE-4076 IC50 increased 475-fold from 184 nM to 87 μM with the SR mutant (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The YW to SR mutation had no effect on slope factor for both voltage-dependent activation or inactivation for either NaV1.2 or NaV1.6.
source: Consistent with prior work studying a similar mutation in NaV1.7 (Ahuja et al., 2015), the YW to SR mutation had no effect on slope factor for both voltage-dependent activation or inactivation for either NaV1.2 or NaV1.6 (Table 2)
evidence: This is based on analysis of activation and inactivation curves presented in Figure 1E and Table 2.

claim: Both voltage-dependent activation and inactivation hyperpolarized by approximately 2 mV for NaV1.6 with the YW to SR mutation, but not NaV1.2.
source: however, both voltage-dependent activation and inactivation hyperpolarized by approximately 2 mV for NaV1.6, but not NaV1.2.
evidence: This is based on analysis of activation and inactivation curves.

claim: In untreated WT conditions, currents recovered to near-baseline levels within 5 s after a 10 s hold at -12 mV.
source: In untreated WT conditions, currents recovered to near-baseline levels within 5 s (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is based on nucleated patch experiments shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons exposed to 200 nM GNE-4076 showed quick recovery similar to untreated WT cells.
source: A similar quick recovery was observed in cells from Scn8a/2aSR/SR mice in the presence of 200 nM GNE-4076.
evidence: This is based on nucleated patch experiments shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: WT neurons exposed to 200 nM GNE-4076 were inhibited markedly, with no appreciable recovery within 25 s.
source: By contrast, WT neurons exposed to the same dosing were inhibited markedly, with no appreciable recovery within 25 s (Figure 1I, J).
evidence: This is based on nucleated patch experiments shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: The AP threshold was hyperpolarized in Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons compared to wildtype cells.
source: However, the AP threshold was hyperpolarized in Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons, likely due to small changes in the voltage dependence of activation observed for heterologously expressed NaV1.6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Table 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AP properties in Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There were no detectable changes to peak dV/dt in Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons compared to wildtype cells.
source: Compared to wildtype cells, there were no detectable changes to peak dV/dt in Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AP properties shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Application with GNE-4076 in either wildtype or Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons had no further effect on threshold or peak dV/dt compared to controls recording in the absence of GNE-4076.
source: Application with GNE-4076 in either wildtype or Scn8a/2aSR/SR neurons had no further effect on threshold or peak dV/dt compared to controls recording in the absence of GNE-4076, suggesting minimal drug binding occurs without marked depolarization or spiking activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AP properties shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 3.

claim: Progressive reduction of NaV1.6 in the compartmental model produced a progressive depolarization of AP threshold and a corresponding decrement in dV/dt throughout the entire rising phase of the AP.
source: Within this model, reducing NaV1.2 or NaV1.6 density had clear, dissociable effects. Progressive reduction of NaV1.6 produced a progressive depolarization of AP threshold and a corresponding decrement in dV/dt throughout the entire rising phase of the AP.
evidence: This is based on compartmental modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NaV1.2 reduction in the compartmental model had no effect on AP threshold or the initial velocity of the AP initiated in the distal AIS.
source: NaV1.2 reduction, by contrast, had no effect on AP threshold or the initial velocity of the AP initiated in the distal AIS.
evidence: This is based on compartmental modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NaV1.2 reduction in the compartmental model impaired components of the AP related to backpropagation and recruitment of somatic NaV channels, with a decrement in peak dV/dt and peak AP membrane potential.
source: Instead, components of the AP related to backpropagation and recruitment of somatic NaV channels were impaired only, with a decrement in peak dV/dt and peak AP membrane potential.
evidence: This is based on compartmental modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When NaV1.6 was blocked, threshold depolarized by 5.8 ± 0.7 mV.
source: When NaV1.6 was blocked, threshold depolarized by 5.8 ± 0.7 mV (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When NaV1.2 was blocked, threshold was unaffected (∆ Vm: –0.1 ± 0.2).
source: When NaV1.2 was blocked instead, threshold was unaffected (∆ Vm: –0.1 ± 0.2).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from experiments.

claim: AP threshold and AP initiation appear to be initiated in an NaV1.6-rich region in control conditions.
source: Thus, AP threshold and AP initiation appear to be initiated in an NaV1.6-rich region in control conditions; but when NaV1.6 is inhibited, APs can occur at more depolarized potentials, likely mediated predominately by NaV1.2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on threshold changes with selective channel block.

claim: The dV/dt at the AIS inflection point was affected only by NaV1.6 block.
source: The dV/dt at the AIS inflection point was affected only by NaV1.6 block (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of the AIS component of the AP shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The dV/dt at the AIS max (trough) was affected by block of either NaV1.2 or NaV1.6.
source: whereas the dV/dt at the trough was affected by block of either isoform (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the AIS component of the AP shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: Acute NaV1.2 block increased AP output.
source: Remarkably, acute NaV1.2 block mirrored conditional knockout and was the only condition in which AP output increased (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Acute NaV1.2 block was associated with a depolarization in afterhyperpolarization voltage.
source: Remarkably, acute NaV1.2 block mirrored conditional knockout and was the only condition in which AP output increased (Figure 4B) and was associated with a depolarization in afterhyperpolarization voltage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NaV1.6 block decreased AP output.
source: In contrast, NaV1.6 block decreased AP output, as did block of both channels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Block of both NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 decreased AP output.
source: In contrast, NaV1.6 block decreased AP output, as did block of both channels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Drug-naive WT neurons responded to somatic current injection with repetitive spiking at a rate of 14.7 ± 0.5 Hz.
source: Drug-naive WT neurons responded to somatic current injection with repetitive spiking at a rate of 14.7 ± 0.5 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from experiments.

claim: In WT neurons treated with GNE-4076, threshold continued to depolarize after the first second, with corresponding decrements in instantaneous frequency and peak AP dV/dt throughout the stimulus.
source: However, in WT neurons treated with GNE-4076, threshold continued to depolarize after the first second, with corresponding decrements in instantaneous frequency and peak AP dV/dt throughout the stimulus (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of prolonged spiking experiments shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: GNE-4076 suppresses firing of neurons with a baseline firing rate of ~15 Hz.
source: This demonstrates that GNE-4076 suppresses firing of neurons with a baseline firing rate of ~15 Hz (Table 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on use-dependent block.

claim: In cases where NaV1.6 alone could be inhibited, AP threshold depolarized in response to GNE-4076 as much as in WT cases.
source: In cases where NaV1.6 alone could be inhibited, AP threshold depolarized in response to GNE-4076 as much as in WT cases (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of selective NaV1.6 block experiments shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: In cases where NaV1.6 alone could be inhibited, AP frequency and peak somatic AP dV/dt were reduced to levels observed in WT cells.
source: Furthermore, AP frequency and peak somatic AP dV/dt were reduced to levels observed in WT cells (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of selective NaV1.6 block experiments shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: In cases where NaV1.2 alone could be inhibited, changes in AP threshold and instantaneous frequency were no different than Scn8a/2aSR/SR conditions.
source: In cases where NaV1.2 alone could be inhibited, changes in AP threshold and instantaneous frequency were no different than Scn8a/2aSR/SR conditions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of selective NaV1.2 block experiments.

claim: The only change in AP properties with selective NaV1.2 block was a decrease in peak AP dV/dt.
source: Indeed, the only change in AP properties was a decrease in peak AP dV/dt (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of selective NaV1.2 block experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: AP threshold and instantaneous frequency are more sensitive to NaV1.6 antagonism.
source: This suggests that AP threshold and instantaneous frequency are more sensitive to NaV1.6 antagonism, whereas peak somatic dV/dt can be affected by antagonism of either isoform.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results comparing selective block of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6.

claim: Peak somatic dV/dt can be affected by antagonism of either NaV1.2 or NaV1.6.
source: This suggests that AP threshold and instantaneous frequency are more sensitive to NaV1.6 antagonism, whereas peak somatic dV/dt can be affected by antagonism of either isoform.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results comparing selective block of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6.

claim: WT cells exposed to GNE-4076 accommodated markedly during seizure-like activity, returning to baseline firing rates at the end of the seizure-like stimulus.
source: WT cells exposed to GNE-4076 accommodated markedly, returning to baseline firing rates at the end of the seizure-like stimulus (Figure 7C, E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of seizure-like activity experiments shown in Figure 7C and 7E.

claim: A less dramatic effect on accommodation was noted when NaV1.6 was blocked alone compared to dual block.
source: A less dramatic effect was noted when NaV1.6 was blocked alone (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of seizure-like activity experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Cells where NaV1.2 could be blocked alone were not appreciably different than untreated controls during seizure-like activity.
source: By contrast, cells where NaV1.2 could be blocked alone were not appreciably different than untreated controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of seizure-like activity experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Some cells with selective NaV1.2 block remained hyperactive compared to control cells throughout the recovery phase.
source: Furthermore, some cells that remained hyperactive with selective NaV1.2 block compared to control cells throughout the recovery phase.
evidence: This is based on analysis of seizure-like activity experiments.

claim: Use-dependent pharmacology that targets NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 may be most beneficial if designed for higher potency at NaV1.6.
source: Together, these data suggest that use-dependent pharmacology that targets NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 may be most beneficial if designed for higher potency at NaV1.6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the seizure-like activity experiments.

claim: Acute blockade of NaV1.6 decreases AP output.
source: Here, we combined genetic and pharmacological strategies to transiently, selectively, and reversibly inhibit either NaV1.6 or NaV1.2 function using activity-dependent ASCs, which bind channels in the inactivated state. We show that acute blockade of either isoform has opposing effects on neuronal output: inhibition of NaV1.6 decreases AP output, whereas NaV1.2 increases AP output.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: Acute blockade of NaV1.2 increases AP output.
source: Here, we combined genetic and pharmacological strategies to transiently, selectively, and reversibly inhibit either NaV1.6 or NaV1.2 function using activity-dependent ASCs, which bind channels in the inactivated state. We show that acute blockade of either isoform has opposing effects on neuronal output: inhibition of NaV1.6 decreases AP output, whereas NaV1.2 increases AP output.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: The block of NaV1.6 rather than NaV1.2 was more effective at tempering spiking activity in cells driven to seizure-like levels of AP output.
source: Given this, we found that the block of NaV1.6 rather than NaV1.2 was more effective at tempering spiking activity in cells driven to seizure-like levels of AP output.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: Pharmacology tuned to preferentially block NaV1.6 over NaV1.2 in a use-dependent manner may be useful as an anti-epileptic.
source: This suggests that pharmacology tuned to preferentially block NaV1.6 over NaV1.2 in a use-dependent manner may be useful as an anti-epileptic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results on seizure-like activity.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings demonstrate that APs initiate ~35–50 µm from the soma, in the distal AIS.
source: Electrophysiological recordings of AP propagation delays between somatic and axonal recordings demonstrate that APs initiate ~35–50 µm from the soma, in the distal AIS (Shu et al., 2007; Palmer and Stuart, 2006; Baranauskas et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The distal AIS is enriched with NaV1.6.
source: This region is enriched with NaV1.6 (Hu et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2014; Royeck et al., 2008; Lorincz and Nusser, 2008; Akin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of NaV1.6 alone alters AP initiation, with an increase in AP threshold and a decrease in total AP number.
source: Consistent with this, we find that inhibition of NaV1.6 alone alters AP initiation, with an increase in AP threshold and a decrease in total AP number from block of this isoform.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Forward propagation of APs is supported almost exclusively by NaV1.6 in nodes of Ranvier and boutons.
source: Forward propagation was not examined here, but prior reports demonstrate that it is supported almost exclusively by NaV1.6 in nodes of Ranvier and boutons (Tian et al., 2014; Caldwell et al., 2000; Kaplan et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Backpropagation through the proximal AIS and soma recruits a mix of NaV1.6 and NaV1.2.
source: By contrast, backpropagation through the proximal AIS and soma recruits a mix of NaV1.6 and NaV1.2.
evidence: This is based on the known distribution of channels and experimental results.

claim: Backpropagation failures were not observed with acute NaV1.2 block.
source: Backpropagation failures were not observed, consistent with results from conditional Scn2a knockout (Spratt et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: A reduction in the velocity at which the AIS component of the AP depolarized was observed when NaV1.2 was blocked selectively.
source: However, we did observe a reduction in the velocity at which the AIS component of the AP depolarized when NaV1.2 was blocked selectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Proximal AIS-localized NaV1.2 aids in boosting backpropagating APs as they transit from the distal AIS to the soma.
source: This suggests that proximal AIS-localized NaV1.2 does aid in boosting backpropagating APs as they transit from the distal AIS to the soma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on selective NaV1.2 block.

claim: NaV1.2 channels are dispensable for recruitment of somatic NaV channels, at least in mouse mPFC layer 5b pyramidal cells.
source: Nevertheless, NaV1.2 channels are still dispensable for recruitment of somatic NaV channels, at least in mouse mPFC layer 5b pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: NaV1.2 expression in pyramidal cell dendrites provides local inward current that boosts dendritic excitability, leading to a recruitment of voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: NaV1.2 expression in pyramidal cell dendrites appears to have two roles in neuronal excitability. Intuitively, these channels provide local inward current that boosts dendritic excitability, leading to a recruitment of voltage-gated calcium channels (Spratt et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dendritic depolarization by NaV1.2 is critical for the recruitment of dendritically localized voltage-gated potassium channels that contribute to AP repolarization and net membrane potential between spikes.
source: But this depolarization also appears to be critical for the recruitment of dendritically localized voltage-gated potassium channels that contribute to AP repolarization and net membrane potential between spikes (Spratt et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Conditional knockout of NaV1.2 paradoxically increases AP output.
source: Indeed, conditional knockout of NaV1.2 paradoxically increases AP output, and we suggested previously that this was due in large part to loss of interactions between dendritic NaV channels and KV channels.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work from the authors.

claim: Identical increases in excitability associated with depolarization of membrane potential between APs could be observed with acute NaV1.2 block.
source: Here, we showed that identical increases in excitability—associated with depolarization of membrane potential between APs—could be observed with acute NaV1.2 block.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Effects of NaV1.2 block on excitability can be due purely to the interplay between dendritic NaV1.2 and KV channels, without modifications to potassium channel distribution or function.
source: This indicates that such effects can be due purely to the interplay between dendritic NaV1.2 and KV channels, and that modifications to potassium channel distribution or function are not necessary for such effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results comparing acute block to conditional knockout.

claim: Knockout of NaV1.6 results in an increase in NaV1.2 expression in the AIS.
source: Similar to NaV1.2 conditional knockout, where NaV1.6 is upregulated, knockout of NaV1.6 results in an increase in NaV1.2 expression, at least in the AIS.
evidence: This statement describes compensatory changes observed in genetic knockout models.

claim: In pyramidal cells from mice constitutively lacking NaV1.6, NaV1.2 occupies the entirety of the AIS rather than just the region proximal to the soma.
source: In pyramidal cells from mice constitutively lacking NaV1.6, NaV1.2 occupies the entirety of the AIS rather than just the region proximal to the soma (Ye et al., 2018; Katz et al., 2018; Royeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acute NaV1.6 block reduces AP output with a concomitant increase in AP threshold.
source: Here, we find that acute NaV1.6 block reduces AP output with a concomitant increase in AP threshold.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Any change in threshold indicates that drugs are interacting with NaV1.6.
source: Of note, this distinction can be leveraged to assess the specificity of other NaV-targeting pharmacology that has been suggested to have specificity at select isoforms, as any change in threshold indicates that drugs are interacting with NaV1.6 (Ye et al., 2018; Filipis et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results that can be used to assess drug specificity.

claim: Compounds similar to GNE-4076 that inhibit both NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 are effective at suppressing chemoconvulsant-induced seizures in ex vivo models.
source: Indeed, compounds similar to those used here that inhibit both NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 (but not other NaV channels) are effective at suppressing chemoconvulsant-induced seizures in ex vivo models (Goodchild et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NaV1.6-preferring ASCs show promise in protecting from chemoconvulsant-induced seizures in vivo.
source: Consistent with this, NaV1.6-preferring ASCs show promise in protecting from chemoconvulsant-induced seizures in vivo (Johnson et al., 2024; Johnson et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A selective ASC for NaV1.6 (NBI-921352) preferentially targets cortical pyramidal cells, unlike carbamazepine that non-selectively targets many NaV isoforms leading to impaired interneuron activity.
source: Similar to our results, Johnson et al. also show that a selective ASC for NaV1.6 (NBI-921352) preferentially targets cortical pyramidal cells, unlike carbamazepine that non-selectively targets many NaV isoforms leading to impaired interneuron activity (Johnson et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Preferential block of NaV1.6 would be beneficial in multiple sodium channelopathy conditions, including those associated with channel loss.
